input:
This passage reports a minimum-stage assessment for a binary distillation separating ethanol and water, carried out at a relative volatility of 2.26, taken as constant over the column. The specifications are a distillate containing 98 mol% of the light component and a bottoms product containing 2 mol% of the light component. Application of the Fenske equation at total reflux gives a minimum stage count of 9.5 theoretical stages, the reboiler included in the count.

This figure is a lower bound on the stages a working column requires. It is calculated at total reflux, where all the condensed vapour returns to the column and no product is withdrawn, so the separation achieved per stage is at its most effective. A column that withdraws product works at a finite reflux and needs more stages for the same specifications; minimum stages and minimum reflux are the two ends of the same trade-off, and a design fixes both quantities away from their limits. For fixed specifications the count is set by the relative volatility: the larger the volatility, the fewer stages the separation requires, and as the volatility approaches unity the stated specifications could not be reached with any practical stage count.

The design reflux ratio is set at 1.3 times the minimum, and the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation rather than from the Fenske relation. Some caution is in order: the minimum count rests on the assumption of a constant relative volatility, whereas the volatility of ethanol and water varies with composition along the column, so the figure of 9.5 stages is only as reliable as that approximation, and it is the simulated count at the design reflux that the design properly rests upon.

A binary distillation separates ethanol and water at a relative volatility of 2.26, taken as constant over the column. The specifications are a distillate of 98 mol% light component and a bottoms of 2 mol% light component. The Fenske equation, applied at total reflux, gives a minimum stage count of 9.5 theoretical stages, the reboiler included in the count.

The figure is a lower bound on the stages a working column needs. It is calculated at total reflux, where the whole of the condensed vapour returns to the column and no product is withdrawn, and separation is at its most effective per stage. A column that withdraws product works at a finite reflux and needs more stages to reach the same specifications; minimum stages and minimum reflux are the two ends of the same trade-off, and a design fixes both quantities away from their limits. Between the specifications, the count is set by the relative volatility: the wider the volatility, the fewer stages the separation needs, and at a volatility close to unity no practical stage count reaches the stated specifications at all.

The design reflux ratio is 1.3 times the minimum, and the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation, not from the Fenske relation. The constant-volatility assumption carries the minimum count: the volatility of ethanol and water varies with composition along the column, so the figure of 9.5 stages is as good as that approximation, and the simulated count at the design reflux is the figure the design rests on.
